The inference about cost-effectiveness requires external information not provided in the passage. Therefore, this option cannot be derived solely from the evidence in the passage.

0.Option: The MDT group exhibited significantly greater bacterial index decline compared to the alternative regimen across all patient subgroups, indicating superior early bactericidal activity of dapsone.
Evidence: Overall, the MDT group demonstrated a more pronounced BI decline trend compared to the alternative regimen (Fig 3a), although this difference did not reach statistical significance.

Patients with aBI < 4 showed no significant differences in BI change between groups (Fig 3b and 3e). However, in the aBI ≥ 4 stratum, the MDT group generally exhibited a higher BI reduction trend than the alternative group, reaching statistical significance particularly in the 4th year, with the decrease rates of 88.64% (MDT) versus 73.22% (alternative) (P = 0.04), albeit marginally significant (Fig 3c).
0.Rationale: The passage states that the MDT group showed a more pronounced BI decline trend but this difference was not statistically significant overall. In the aBI ≥ 4 subgroup, the difference was marginally significant (P = 0.04). 0.Option: Dapsone-free alternative regimens demonstrated comparable clinical efficacy to standard MDT in multibacillary leprosy patients, despite a non-significantly longer treatment duration and slower bacterial index decline in the high-bacillary load subgroup.
Evidence: No significant between-group differences were observed at any timepoint (P = 0.06 and 0.80, respectively; Fig 2a and S1 Table). Additionally, we also performed Cox regression adjusting for age, sex, disease duration, aBI, and treatment regimen. Only aBI significantly influenced cure rates (HR = 0.76, P < 0.001) and acted as a risk factor (S2 Table). Stratified analyses by aBI (< 4 and ≥ 4; Fig 2b and 2c) and subsequent Cox regression confirmed no significant treatment effect within either strata (all P > 0.05; S3 Table), indicating equivalent clinical cure efficacy between alternative therapy and MDT across bacterial load levels.

Mean treatment duration was 1.68 (±0.69) years (alternative, n = 111) versus 1.60 (±0.64) years (MDT, n = 148), with no significant difference (P = 0.37; Fig 2d). Stratification by aBI also revealed no intergroup disparities between groups (aBI < 4: 1.58 vs. 1.56 years, P = 0.80; aBI ≥ 4: 1.84 vs. 1.66 years, P = 0.16; Fig 2e and 2f).

In the aBI ≥ 4 stratum, the MDT group generally exhibited a higher BI reduction trend than the alternative group, reaching statistical significance particularly in the 4th year, with the decrease rates of 88.64% (MDT) versus 73.22% (alternative) (P = 0.04), albeit marginally significant (Fig 3c).
0.Rationale: The passage provides evidence that dapsone-free alternative regimens demonstrated comparable clinical efficacy to standard MDT in multibacillary leprosy patients. Cure rates were not significantly different between groups at any timepoint, and stratified analyses by aBI confirmed no significant treatment effect. Treatment duration was also not significantly different. In the high-bacillary load subgroup (aBI ≥ 4), the MDT group showed a higher BI reduction trend, but the difference was only marginally significant. Therefore, the option is correct as it accurately reflects the findings of the study.

Therefore, this option cannot be derived from the passage.

1.Option: The high phase coherence between local climate variables and dengue incidence in most provinces indicates that climate-based early warning systems can be uniformly implemented across Indonesia with minimal adaptation.
Evidence: Phase coherence exceeded 0.85 in 19 provinces for precipitation and 9 for temperature (Fig 5B). This threshold, while necessarily arbitrary, identifies provinces where climate-dengue timing is sufficiently consistent for early warning.
Provinces with both positive or zero lag (after rounding) and high coherence are selected as candidates for climate-based risk prediction (18 for precipitation and 7 for temperature).
1.Rationale: The passage explicitly states that phase coherence exceeding 0.85 was observed in only 19 provinces for precipitation and 9 for temperature, not 'most provinces'. The option incorrectly claims that climate-based early warning systems can be uniformly implemented with minimal adaptation, but the data show significant regional variation in phase coherence. The passage also notes that only 18 provinces for precipitation and 7 for temperature were identified as candidates for climate-based risk prediction, indicating that a uniform approach would not be appropriate across Indonesia.

1.Option: The strong association between El Niño events and elevated dengue outbreak risk suggests that national-level strategic preparedness based on ENSO monitoring can effectively predict and prevent all major dengue outbreaks across Indonesia.
Evidence: The mean incidence during strong El Niño years was 96% higher than in non-strong El Niño years (77 vs 39 per 100,000). The strongest El Niño (2015–2016, average ONI–1.81) preceded the 2015–2016 outbreak peak.

Of the two regional climate indices, ONI showed a stronger association with epidemic-year incidence (ρ–0.83; p–<0.01) than DMI (ρ–0.33; p–0.25), based on correlations between July-June averaged index values and corresponding annual incidence.

Regional variation was observed, with ONI correlations being highest in Kalimantan (ρ–0.90) and Sulawesi (ρ–0.83), whereas DMI exhibited stronger associations than ONI in Maluku (ρ–0.60 vs 0.29) and Nusa Tenggara (ρ–0.46 vs 0.32) (Table G in S1 Appendix).
1.Rationale: While the passage confirms a strong association between El Niño events and elevated dengue risk, it also shows regional variation in these associations. The option incorrectly claims that ENSO monitoring can 'effectively predict and prevent all major dengue outbreaks', but the data show that DMI (Indian Ocean Dipole) has stronger associations in some regions (Maluku, Nusa Tenggara) than ONI. The passage also notes that the multi-annual outbreak peaks coincided with El Niño conditions, but this does not imply that all outbreaks can be predicted or prevented through ENSO monitoring alone. The regional variation in climate-dengue relationships undermines the claim of a uniform national-level strategy.

1.Option: The west-to-east gradient in dengue outbreak timing is robust in western Indonesia but breaks down in eastern Indonesia, indicating that climate-driven seasonality patterns differ significantly across the archipelago.
Evidence: Wavelet analysis revealed a systematic west-to-east gradient in annual dengue wave timing (Fig 2A; mean with 2.5th-97.5th percentile ranges of pairwise differences are available in Fig B in S1 Appendix). Provinces in Sumatra and western Kalimantan showed negative phase lags (averaging peaks 1.4 months earlier than the national average), while Java-Bali and eastern Kalimantan (averaging peaks 0.8 months later) and eastern provinces (averaging peaks 0.1 months later) showed positive phase lags.

The gradient’s strength varied by geographic scope (Table 1). The west-to-east gradient, as measured by Spearman correlations, was strongest for western provinces only (Sumatra–Java-Bali; median Spearman rho–0.7, significant across all years), weaker when Kalimantan was included, and weakest across all provinces.
Dynamic time warping (DTW) clustering showed that dengue incidence heterogeneity is too complex for simple geographic regionalisation, especially in eastern Indonesia.

Temporal similarity within geographical regions varied substantially (Fig 3D and Table 2). The Nusa Tenggara region (two provinces) showed the highest cohesion (mean DTW distance–82.7), while the Papua region (two provinces) showed the lowest.
1.Rationale: The passage provides multiple lines of evidence supporting this conclusion. The wavelet analysis shows a clear west-to-east gradient in dengue timing that is strongest in western Indonesia. The gradient weakens when including Kalimantan and becomes weakest across all provinces. The DTW clustering analysis further confirms that dengue patterns in eastern Indonesia are too complex for simple geographic regionalisation. The passage explicitly states that the gradient's strength varies by geographic scope, with the strongest correlation in western provinces. This directly supports the inference that climate-driven seasonality patterns differ significantly across the archipelago, particularly between western and eastern regions.

1.Option: Dengue transmission in Indonesia is primarily driven by temperature, as high temperature was associated with significantly elevated cumulative risk in most provinces with reliable climate-dengue timing relationships.
Evidence: For the following phase and dose-response analyses, we focused on precipitation and temperature, excluding relative humidity due to its high correlation with precipitation and similar but delayed phase patterns.

For provinces with reliable climate-dengue timing (coherence ≥0.85 and positive or zero lag), high precipitation (90th vs. 50th percentile) was associated with significantly elevated cumulative risk in 11 of 18 qualified provinces at their wavelet-derived optimal lag (Fig 6A). Median cumulative elevated risk for 90th percentile precipitation ranged from 21-95%, and lag timing varied from 0-3 months at statistically significant provinces.

For temperature, 3 of 7 qualifying provinces showed significant effects, with one (West Nusa Tenggara) showing reduced cumulative risk at the wavelet-derived optimal lag (Fig 6B). Median cumulative elevated risk for the 90th percentile temperature ranged from 111-236%, and lag timing varied from 0-3 months at statistically significant provinces.
1.Rationale: The passage shows that precipitation was associated with significantly elevated cumulative risk in 11 of 18 qualified provinces, while temperature showed significant effects in only 3 of 7 qualifying provinces. The option incorrectly claims that temperature is the primary driver, but the data clearly show that precipitation has a more consistent and widespread association with dengue risk. The passage also notes that relative humidity was excluded due to its high correlation with precipitation, further supporting the importance of precipitation over temperature in dengue transmission dynamics.

1.Option: The breakdown of the west-to-east dengue timing gradient in eastern Indonesia is primarily due to underreporting in surveillance systems, which leads to inaccurate phase lag estimates in those regions.
Evidence: Dynamic time warping (DTW) clustering showed that dengue incidence heterogeneity is too complex for simple geographic regionalisation, especially in eastern Indonesia.

Temporal similarity within geographical regions varied substantially (Fig 3D and Table 2). The Nusa Tenggara region (two provinces) showed the highest cohesion (mean DTW distance–82.7), while the Papua region (two provinces) showed the lowest.

The study period encompassed 2 strong El Niño events (2015–2016 and 2023–2024, averaging >1 ONI) and 1 strong La Niña event (2010–2011, averaging–<–1 ONI) (Fig 4A). The multi-annual outbreak peaks identified in Fig 1B coincided with strong El Niño conditions.
We excluded four provinces established in 2022 from the reorganisation of Papua (South Papua, Central Papua, Highland Papua, and Southwest Papua) due to substantial missing data.
1.Rationale: The passage provides no evidence that the breakdown of the west-to-east gradient in eastern Indonesia is due to underreporting. Instead, it attributes the complexity to the inherent heterogeneity of dengue patterns in eastern Indonesia. The exclusion of four provinces from the analysis is noted, but this is specifically for Papua provinces established in 2022 due to missing data, not for the entire eastern region. The DTW clustering analysis explicitly states that dengue incidence heterogeneity is too complex for simple regionalisation in eastern Indonesia, which is presented as a finding rather than a limitation due to underreporting.

2.Option: The explosive growth in brucellosis incidence from 2007 to 2015, followed by a brief decline and resurgent rise, indicates that the epidemic is primarily driven by seasonal fluctuations in animal husbandry and human mobility.
Evidence: The study period (2007–2022) was marked by a 167-fold increase in overall incidence rate, from 0.52 to 86.83 per 100,000 population.

Joinpoint regression analysis delineated three distinct phases: a period of rapid increase from 2007 to 2015, a brief interim decline from 2015 to 2018, and a subsequent resurgent rise from 2018 to 2022.

2.Rationale: The passage describes a dramatic 167-fold increase in incidence over the study period, with three distinct phases identified through joinpoint analysis. However, the option incorrectly attributes this pattern to 'seasonal fluctuations in animal husbandry and human mobility.' The passage explicitly links the epidemic to long-term socioeconomic and livestock production factors, not seasonal variations. The spatial evolution from low and homogeneous to a defined high-risk zone further supports a systemic rather than seasonal driver.

2.Option: The U-shaped risk pattern observed for sheep inventory suggests that both extensive and intensive sheep farming systems are equally high-risk, requiring identical intervention strategies focused on biosecurity and surveillance.
Evidence: The final DLNM revealed distinct temporal patterns of association. For sheep inventory, a 'U-shaped' risk pattern emerged across the lag dimension, where both extremely low and high standardized inventory levels were associated with increased risk at specific lag periods.
Interaction detector analysis revealed that the combined influence of two factors often resulted in a nonlinear, enhanced effect greater than the sum of their individual impacts.
2.Rationale: The passage describes a U-shaped risk pattern for sheep inventory but does not state that extensive and intensive systems are 'equally high-risk' or require 'identical intervention strategies.' The nonlinear relationship and interaction effects suggest complex dynamics that may require differentiated approaches. The option overgeneralizes the findings and misrepresents the nuanced, context-dependent risk patterns identified in the study.

2.Option: The epidemic’s trajectory, defined by a high-risk cluster strongly associated with livestock scale and modulated by lagged and immediate socioeconomic factors, reflects a systemic failure in integrating health security with economic development in pastoral regions.

The DLNM revealed that increases in cattle inventory were associated with a peak in relative risk at a three-year lag, while increases in regional GDP exhibited a protective effect.

2.Option: The persistent high-risk cluster in central and eastern Ningxia, associated with a 4.22-fold higher relative risk, is primarily driven by unhygienic milking and processing of raw milk products, which are common in small-scale dairy operations.

This inference is directly supported by the study's findings and the passage's discussion of the One Health framework.

3.Option: The presence of Leishmania infantum DNA in a clinically healthy maned wolf, combined with high vector density in its enclosure, indicates that captive wild animals in urban zoos are likely to serve as primary reservoirs for visceral leishmaniasis transmission.
Evidence: The detection of Leishmania infantum DNA in a maned wolf (Chrysocyon brachyurus; sample no. 19, ID 245565) confirms the presence of the parasite in a zoo-housed wild carnivore.
The role of zoo-housed mammals in the maintenance of VL transmission cycles therefore remains poorly understood, representing a critical gap in One Health surveillance.
3.Rationale: While the study confirms the presence of Leishmania infantum in a zoo-housed maned wolf, it does not provide evidence that this animal is a primary reservoir for visceral leishmaniasis transmission. 3.Option: The discordant results between qPCR and the other two molecular assays suggest that qPCR is unreliable for detecting Leishmania infantum in captive wildlife, rendering it unsuitable for use in zoo surveillance programs.

This single instance does not provide sufficient evidence to conclude that qPCR is unreliable for detecting Leishmania infantum in captive wildlife. The option overgeneralizes from a single data point and makes an unsupported claim about the suitability of qPCR for zoo surveillance programs. The study does not evaluate the overall reliability of qPCR in this context.

3.Option: The detection of Leishmania infantum in a maned wolf at the Belo Horizonte Zoo confirms that urban zoos are the primary source of visceral leishmaniasis outbreaks in surrounding human populations.
Evidence: The detection of Leishmania infantum DNA in a maned wolf (Chrysocyon brachyurus; sample no. 19, ID 245565) confirms the presence of the parasite in a zoo-housed wild carnivore.
The role of zoo-housed mammals in the maintenance of VL transmission cycles therefore remains poorly understood, representing a critical gap in One Health surveillance.
3.Rationale: The study detects Leishmania infantum in a zoo-housed maned wolf but does not establish that urban zoos are the primary source of visceral leishmaniasis outbreaks in surrounding human populations. 3.Option: Because the maned wolf was found to be infected with Leishmania infantum, zoos in endemic areas should immediately implement mandatory quarantine and culling of all wild carnivores to prevent disease spread.
Evidence: The detection of Leishmania infantum DNA in a maned wolf (Chrysocyon brachyurus; sample no. 19, ID 245565) confirms the presence of the parasite in a zoo-housed wild carnivore.
All animal handling and sampling procedures were conducted in accordance with the institutional animal welfare, biosafety, and veterinary care protocols of the Belo Horizonte Zoo.
3.Rationale: The study detects Leishmania infantum in a zoo-housed maned wolf but does not provide evidence to support the claim that zoos should implement mandatory quarantine and culling of all wild carnivores. 4.Option: The endorsement of harmful traditional practices by Public Health Midwives is a direct result of their lack of confidence in managing snakebites, which undermines their ability to apply correct first-aid knowledge.
Evidence: A majority indicated that they would suck out the venom (71.6%), apply herbs (73.2%), or make an incision at the bite site (64.4%).
Approximately, 40% endorsed applying a tournquet as an appropriate first-aid technique, while 59.9% stated they would not recommend any first aid at all.

Bivariate analysis showed that PHMs who had previously received first-aid training, were aware of national information services or treatment guidelines, or had higher confidence in managing snakebites were significantly more likely to possess adequate knowledge (p < 0.001).
4.Rationale: The passage provides evidence that endorsement of harmful traditional practices is widespread among PHMs, but it does not establish a direct causal relationship between this endorsement and lack of confidence. In fact, the bivariate analysis shows that higher confidence is associated with better knowledge. The passage also notes that many PHMs (59.9%) would not recommend any first aid at all, which suggests that lack of confidence may lead to inaction rather than endorsement of harmful practices. The claim of a direct causal relationship is not supported by the evidence presented.

PHMs with adequate first-aid knowledge were significantly more likely to correctly identify snakes and to be aware of their venomous status (p < 0.001).

Those with adequate knowledge of snakebite first-aid were significantly more likely to have received first-aid training, to be aware of national information services and guidelines, and to have prior experience providing first aid to a child with snakebite.
4.Rationale: While the passage does show poor snake identification skills, it does not attribute this to insufficient access to visual training materials during midwifery education. Instead, it links identification skills to first-aid knowledge, training history, and experience. The passage specifically notes that PHMs with adequate first-aid knowledge were more likely to correctly identify snakes, suggesting that the issue is broader than just access to visual materials. The claim about midwifery education specifically is not supported by the evidence presented.

Evidence: Most PHMs correctly recognised the importance of reassuring and calming the victim (95.9%) and transporting the child promptly to a hospital with antivenom facilities (95.8%).
A majority indicated that they would suck out the venom (71.6%), apply herbs (73.2%), or make an incision at the bite site (64.4%).
Approximately, 40% endorsed applying a tournquet as an appropriate first-aid technique, while 59.9% stated they would not recommend any first aid at all.

It shows that while PHMs have high awareness of basic principles like reassurance and prompt transport (95.9% and 95.8% respectively), a majority endorse harmful traditional practices such as venom sucking (71.6%), herb application (73.2%), and incision (64.4%). This directly demonstrates a significant discrepancy between theoretical knowledge of modern first-aid principles and actual practices that PHMs would implement in real-world scenarios.

4.Option: The widespread endorsement of traditional practices among Public Health Midwives suggests that cultural beliefs are the primary driver of health-seeking behavior in rural Sri Lanka, overshadowing formal medical knowledge.

In the Sri Lankan context, where healthcare access and health-seeking behaviour are strongly influenced by community-level health workers, assessing PHMs’ knowledge and practices represents an essential step toward strengthening pre-hospital care and prevention of paediatric snakebites.
4.Rationale: While the passage acknowledges the persistence of traditional practices, it does not claim that cultural beliefs are the primary driver of health-seeking behavior. 4.Option: The high rate of correct responses on evidence-based first-aid measures indicates that Public Health Midwives in Sri Lanka are well-prepared to manage paediatric snakebites in real-world settings.
Evidence: Most PHMs correctly recognised the importance of reassuring and calming the victim (95.9%) and transporting the child promptly to a hospital with antivenom facilities (95.8%).
A majority indicated that they would suck out the venom (71.6%), apply herbs (73.2%), or make an incision at the bite site (64.4%).
Overall, fewer than half of the respondents demonstrated adequate first-aid knowledge according to the scoring criteria (Table 1).
4.Rationale: The passage shows that while PHMs have high awareness of some evidence-based measures (95.9% for reassurance, 95.8% for prompt transport), the overall assessment indicates that fewer than half demonstrated adequate first-aid knowledge. The high rate of correct responses on specific measures does not translate to overall preparedness, especially given the widespread endorsement of harmful traditional practices. The claim that PHMs are 'well-prepared' is not supported by the evidence presented.

Five ES genes encoded glutathione S-transferase, an enzyme thought to detoxify free heme generated during hemoglobin proteolysis and other toxins [40,90]. Sixteen ES genes encoded Stichodactyla helianthus toxin (ShK)-related proteins, which might suppress host T cells [91,92]; and nine ES genes encoded C-type lectin proteins, which might mimic mammalian immune proteins (enabling immunosuppression) or dissociate cells (enabling tissue invasion) [25,26,54,93,94].

ES genes also encode three other multigene families of secreted proteins that are suspected to be involved in infection, although their molecular roles remain largely uncharacterized: ASP-related (ASPR), transthyretin-like (TTL), and secreted clade V proteins (SCVP). ASPRs were first observed in A. ceylanicum as a divergent subfamily of ASPs transcriptionally upregulated immediately after host infection [54], and were later observed in ES proteins from N. americanus [44]. TTL proteins were previously observed as a major component of ES proteins from H. contortus [47] and as multigene families in several parasitic nematodes [100–102]; one TTL protein of H. contortus (HcTTR) antagonizes goat IL-4 in vitro, and thus may be immunosuppressive in vivo [103]. SCVPs were observed in A. ceylanicum as a novel family of secreted proteins upregulated in young hookworm adults that is conserved in C. elegans and expanded in hookworms and other strongylids [54].

Although we have focused on analyzing our own ES gene set, we have also identified statistically enriched protein domains for the 955 adult ES genes identified by Uzoechi et al. and Wong et al. (both involving Washington University, and thus collectively labeled “WashU”) and for their 511 ES genes not found in our data set (“WashU-only”; S3 Table). Domains preferentially enriched in WashU-only ES genes include aminopeptidases, fatty acid- and retinol-binding (FAR) proteins, SXP/RAL-2 proteins, and C-type lectins (Table 3). Aminopeptidases may cooperate with the five other protease types noted above to enable digestion and immunosuppression. FAR proteins are a nematode-specific protein family that may suppress immune responses in plant or animal hosts by sequestering lipid signaling molecules [104–106]. The SXP/RAL-2 protein family includes homologs of an immunodominant hypodermal antigen found in several parasitic nematodes: Ac16, in the dog hookworm A. caninum [107]; both As16 and As14, in the roundworm Ascaris suum [108–110]; Ani s 5 in the ascaridoid Anisakis simplex [111]; and Ov-RAL-2 in the filarial parasite Onchocerca volvulus [112]. Among the C-type lectins enriched in WashU-only ES genes, we observed two genes encoding structural mimics of mammalian mannose receptor (Table 4) [54]; in mammals, this receptor binds soluble secreted molecules from the whipworm Trichuris suis and from A. suum, and these A. ceylanicum mimics might thus be immunomodulatory [113]. Conversely, domains preferentially enriched in our ES genes included CAP, ASPR, cysteine protease, astacin, Kunitz protease inhibitor, ShK, TTL, and SCVP domains (Table 3).

Other ES genes we observed were potentially relevant to infection despite not being from overrepresented families (Table 4). One encodes a macin homolog that may protect hookworms from being infected by bacteria, and thus enable their long-term residence in the human gut [114,115]. Three ES homologs of A. caninum anticoagulant protein [116] could act with Acey-HPI to prevent clotting during blood feeding. Seven other ES genes encode possible immunosuppressants: two ES apyrases and one ES adenosine deaminase could suppress both blood clotting and inflammation by hydrolyzing extracellular ATP [117–119]; phospholipases A2 and D, like FAR proteins, could suppress lipid signals in immune responses [120]; the ES macrophage migration inhibitory factor Acey-MIF-1, previously observed to bind the human MIF receptor CD74 and promote monocyte migration, could alter cellular immune responses [121,122]; and an ES deoxyribonuclease II could hydrolyze extracellular DNA nets secreted by neutrophils to trap and kill large pathogens [123].

Because ES proteins are exposed to the human host’s immune system and are likely to promote infection, ES proteins are promising targets for an anti-hookworm vaccine. Twelve ES genes encoded proteins that have already been shown to give partial protection as vaccines in laboratory mammals, or to be homologous to such proteins (Table 4): the cysteine protease Acey-CP-1 [124]; the M13 peptidases Acey-MEP-6 and Acey-MEP-7 [125,126]; the glutathione S-transferase Acey-GST-1, homologous to A. caninum’s Acan-GST-1 [127] and N. americanus’ Na-GST-1 [128]; a homolog of the immunodominant hypodermal Ac-16 antigen of A. caninum [107]; two homologs of apyrases in Teledorsagia circumcincta and H. bakeri [129,130]; two homologs of fatty acid- and retinol-binding proteins in A. ceylanicum [131] and Onchocerca volvulus [132]; one homolog of Brugia malayi calreticulin [133]; one homolog of Onchocerca volvulus fructose-1,6-bisphosphate aldolase [134]; and one homolog to A. suum enolase [135]. In addition to these strict orthologs, three instances of astacin, ASP, and TTL proteins (all overrepresented among ES proteins) have given partial protection as vaccines: Ac-MTP-1 of A. caninum, Acan-ASP-2 of A. caninum, and HcTTR of H. contortus [136–138]. Finally, two WashU-only ES genes encoded homologs of an extracellular Argonaute (exWAGO) protein in H. bakeri that binds small RNAs, is imported by mouse cells during infection with possible immunomodulatory effects, and confers partial protection as a vaccine in mice [139]; a third WashU-only ES gene encoded the aspartic protease Acey-APR-1, homologous to the vaccine subunit Na-APR-1 from N. americanus [140]. These results show the vaccine potential of ES proteins, with hundreds of other ES proteins remaining untested as vaccine subunits.

Over half of A. ceylanicum ES genes are functionally conserved in related blood-feeding parasitic nematodes: they do not merely have orthologs, but ES gene orthologs (Tables 5, S1, and S7). Out of 565 A. ceylanicum ES genes, 269 (47.6%) had ES gene orthologs in the closely related hookworm A. caninum [45], 21-fold more than expected by chance (p = 6.82•10-301). For the more distantly related hookworm N. americanus [44], 141/565 ES genes (25.0%) had ES gene orthologs (18-fold over chance; p = 1.78•10-137); for the still more distantly related blood-feeding H. contortus [47], 180/565 ES genes (31.9%) had ES gene orthologs (8.9-fold over chance, p = 4.10•10-120). Considering all three species at once, 350/565 ES genes (61.9%) had some ES ortholog (12-fold over chance, p = 0). We found similarly high conservation for the 860 ES genes described by Uzoechi et al. (S7 Table), and overrepresented ES gene orthologies between A. ceylanicum and N. americanus were also observed by Uzoechi et al. [58]. These orthologies of A. ceylanicum ES genes in other species are predominantly to ES genes themselves (i.e., genes experimentally shown to encode ES proteins in these other species). When ES genes in other species are set aside, the remaining orthologies of A. ceylanicum ES genes fall to, or even below, background frequencies. For A. ceylanicum ES genes without known ES gene orthologs, orthology to A. caninum dropped to 1.6-fold over chance (p = 1.31•10-29); in N. americanus, to 1.1-fold below chance (p = 0.22); and in H. contortus, to 2.4-fold below chance (p = 2.05•10-30). Thus, the A. ceylanicum ES gene set predominantly encodes ES proteins not only in A. ceylanicum itself but also in related parasitic nematodes.

The 153 positively immunoregulated intestinal ES genes disproportionately encoded astacin proteases, TIMP and TIL protease inhibitors, ShK-like proteins, ASPs, ASPRs, and SCVPs (Table 10 and Fig 11). Of these genes, 69 had ES gene orthologs in A. caninum (20-fold enrichment; p = 6.00•10-72), 24 in N. americanus (11-fold enrichment; p = 2.35•10-18), and 24 in H. contortus (4.4-fold enrichment; p = 1.23•10-9; S14 Table). As noted above, all of the above protein families may affect immunomodulation in hookworm hosts; in addition, astacin has been shown to enable tissue invasion in vitro by A. caninum [86]. Other immunoregulated ES genes also encoded proteins with possible functions in immunoregulation, antithrombosis, or digesting host tissue (S1 Table): the ASPs Acey-NIF-B [97,98] and Acey-HPI [99], two apyrases [118,119], deoxyribonuclease II [123], hyaluronidase [180,181], and superoxide dismutase [182,183].

This UpSet plot shows, for the set of 153 positively immunoregulated intestinal ES genes, occurrences of seven Pfam domains overrrepresented in that set (Table 10). The x-axis, y-axis, and matrix are as in Fig 3, except that the genes being considered are not only ES protein-coding but also positively immunoregulated in the 19-day intestine. Abbreviations for Pfam domains are given in Table 10. Not shown are an additional 53 positively immunoregulated intestinal ES genes that lacked any of these seven overrepresented Pfam domains. The domain patterns are a subset of those observed for ES genes alone (Fig 3), and represent possible virulence factors in the ES gene set.
